title: Relational Algebra & SQL Mastery
intro: Relational algebra and SQL: queries, views, procedures, triggers and injection defence.

sec.s: A relational database organizes information into tables.

b.x: A relational database organizes information into tables. A table represents a category of facts, such as students, courses, products, or orders. Each table has columns describing properties and rows containing individual records. Tables can be connected through keys, allowing a database to represent real-world relationships without placing every fact in one large table.

STUDENT stores student details, COURSE stores course details, and ENROLMENT connects students with courses. The student_id and course_id columns in ENROLMENT can be foreign keys referencing the other tables.

A query asks a database to return or modify information. SQL, or Structured Query Language, is widely used to communicate with relational database systems. Relational algebra is a formal mathematical foundation for expressing operations on relations. Studying both makes it easier to understand what a query means and how relational data is processed.

x: Tuple: a row in a relation.
Attribute: a named property, commonly represented as a column.
Domain: the permitted type or set of values for an attribute.
Schema: the defined structure of database objects.
Query: a request to retrieve or manipulate data.
Predicate: a condition that can be evaluated as true, false, or, with SQL NULL semantics, unknown.
Join: an operation that combines related rows from two relations or tables.

b.x: Classical relational theory treats relations as sets of tuples, while SQL tables can contain duplicate rows unless uniqueness is enforced. SQL also includes NULL and practical features that differ from the simplest mathematical relational model. These differences matter when translating formal expressions into real SQL.

sec.s: Relational algebra is a formal query language and mathematical system used to operate on relations.

b.x: Relational algebra is a formal query language and mathematical system used to operate on relations. Its operations take one or more relations as input and produce a relation as output. This property is called closure: the output of an operation can become the input of another operation.
A complex query can therefore be built by combining smaller operations. For example, one can select students belonging to BCA and then project only their names.

x: Understand the mathematical foundation of relational databases.
Express filtering, column selection, and record combination.
Break complex queries into smaller steps.
Understand how formal theory relates to SQL.

b.x: Common operations include selection, projection, union, set difference, Cartesian product, rename, join, intersection, and division. This guide concentrates on selection, projection, and joins, while briefly explaining the others.

sec.s: Selection chooses rows from a relation that satisfy a condition.

b.x: Selection chooses rows from a relation that satisfy a condition. It is represented by the Greek lowercase letter sigma: σ.
This means: return rows from STUDENT for which age is at least 19.
Selection filters rows; it does not normally remove columns. All attributes of qualifying rows remain in the result.
The WHERE clause expresses the condition. The asterisk requests all columns.

In common SQL pattern syntax, % matches zero or more characters and _ matches one character. Case sensitivity depends on the DBMS, collation, and configuration.
NULL represents a missing, unknown, or inapplicable value. It is not the same as zero or an empty string. Do not use age = NULL to test for NULL.
SQL uses three-valued logic for many expressions involving NULL: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause returns rows for which the condition is TRUE; FALSE and UNKNOWN rows are not returned.

sec.s: Projection selects specified attributes or columns from a relation.

b.x: Projection selects specified attributes or columns from a relation. It is represented by the Greek uppercase letter pi: π.
Projection changes which columns are returned. In classical relational algebra, relations are sets, so duplicate tuples are removed. SQL normally retains duplicates unless DISTINCT is specified.
Without DISTINCT, BCA may appear multiple times because several students belong to that department.
Selection chooses rows. Projection chooses columns.

x: “Show all students who are 19 or older” is selection.
“Show only student names and departments” is projection.
“Show names of BCA students aged 19 or older” combines both.

sec.s: A relational database usually stores different categories of facts in separate tables.

b.x: A relational database usually stores different categories of facts in separate tables. STUDENT stores names, COURSE stores course names, and ENROLMENT connects the two using identifiers. A join combines related rows so that an application can retrieve information across these tables.
The query matches enrolment rows to students and courses by their identifiers. One student can appear multiple times if they have multiple enrolments.
A theta join combines tuples from two relations when a specified comparison condition is satisfied. The condition may use =, <, >, ≤, or ≥.
A theta join can be understood as a selection applied to a Cartesian product.
An equi-join uses equality conditions to match rows.
Both join columns may be selected if desired. An equi-join is a common special case of a theta join.
An INNER JOIN returns rows for which the join condition matches in both tables.
Students without an enrolment are not returned because no matching enrolment row exists. In many SQL dialects, JOIN by itself means INNER JOIN.
A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and matching rows from the right table. If no match exists, right-side columns contain NULL.
This includes students who have no enrolment.
To find students with no enrolment

This is an anti-join pattern. Be careful: placing a right-table filter in WHERE can remove unmatched rows and effectively change the result toward an inner join. Depending on the goal, the filter may belong in the ON clause.

A RIGHT JOIN returns every row from the right table and matching rows from the left table. Unmatched left-side columns become NULL. Support varies by DBMS; some systems do not implement RIGHT JOIN. Reversing the table order and using LEFT JOIN can often achieve the same result.

A FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched rows and unmatched rows from both sides, with NULLs where no match exists. Support varies by DBMS and version. Check the database product's documentation before relying on it.
A Cartesian product combines every row from one relation with every row from another. If R has 3 rows and S has 4 rows, the product has 3 × 4 = 12 combinations.

This creates every student-course combination whether or not the student is enrolled in the course. A cross join can be useful for generating combinations, but an accidental missing join condition can produce a huge result.

A NATURAL JOIN automatically matches columns with the same names in both tables. This can be risky if similarly named columns are not intended to match, or if future schema changes add another same-named column. Explicit JOIN ... ON conditions are often clearer and safer.
A self join joins a table to itself. It is useful when rows refer to other rows in the same table.
E and M are aliases representing different roles for the same table.

sec.s: Union combines tuples from two union-compatible relations.

b.x: Union combines tuples from two union-compatible relations. Their corresponding attributes must have compatible domains.
UNION normally removes duplicates. UNION ALL retains duplicates and can be faster because it avoids duplicate elimination.
Set difference returns tuples in one relation that are not in another.
This returns student IDs in Student that do not appear in Enrolment, subject to the DBMS's set-operation semantics.
Intersection returns tuples common to both compatible relations. Some DBMS products support INTERSECT. It can also be expressed using other operations.
Rename changes a relation or attribute name in relational algebra. SQL aliases provide a similar practical convenience:

Relational division expresses “for all” queries. For example, “Find students enrolled in every required course.” SQL can express such queries using NOT EXISTS or grouping and counting. Care is needed around empty sets, duplicate rows, and the definition of “required course.”

sec.s: SQL stands for Structured Query Language.

b.x: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is used to define relational database structures, insert and modify data, retrieve results, control permissions, and manage transactions, depending on the DBMS and dialect.
SQL is declarative: the user generally specifies what result is wanted rather than describing every low-level step. The DBMS query optimizer chooses an execution plan.
SQL dialects vary. SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle share much syntax but differ in data types, date handling, stored procedures, triggers, and other features.
DDL: Data Definition Language. Defines or changes structures. Common commands: CREATE, ALTER, DROP.

DML: Data Manipulation Language. Inserts, updates, or deletes rows. Common commands: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. SELECT is often classified separately as DQL, although some courses include it under a broad DML category.
DQL: Data Query Language. Commonly refers to SELECT queries.
DCL: Data Control Language. Manages permissions, with commands such as GRANT and REVOKE in systems that support them.
TCL: Transaction Control Language. Includes COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
The classifications can vary between textbooks. Understanding each command's purpose is more important than memorizing a single classification scheme.

sec.s: A nested query, or subquery, is a query placed inside another SQL statement.

b.x: A nested query, or subquery, is a query placed inside another SQL statement. The outer query uses the inner query's result. Subqueries can appear in WHERE, HAVING, FROM, SELECT, and in data-changing statements where the DBMS supports the syntax.
A scalar subquery returns one value: one row and one column.
The inner query calculates the average age. The outer query returns students older than that average.
If a scalar subquery returns more than one row, systems that require a single value may raise an error. Exact behavior depends on the DBMS and context.
The inner query returns the maximum credit value, and the outer query finds courses with that value.
IN checks whether a value matches one of the values returned by a subquery.
This returns students enrolled in course 10.
NOT IN can behave unexpectedly if the subquery returns NULL. SQL's three-valued logic may make the condition UNKNOWN rather than TRUE.
When checking that no related row exists, NOT EXISTS is often clearer.
This returns students for whom no matching enrolment exists. The subquery is correlated because it refers to S.student_id from the outer query.
EXISTS is true when the subquery returns at least one row.
This returns courses with at least one enrolment. SELECT 1 is conventional because EXISTS cares about whether a row exists, not which columns are returned.
A correlated subquery refers to a value from the outer query. It is conceptually evaluated in relation to each candidate outer row, though the optimizer may transform it into another execution plan.
The subquery checks whether each student has an active enrolment.
Some SQL systems support comparisons with ALL or ANY (also called SOME in some contexts).
salary > ALL (subquery) means the salary is greater than every value returned.
salary > ANY (subquery) means the salary is greater than at least one returned value.
Behavior with empty results and NULLs requires care. Equivalent queries using aggregates or EXISTS may sometimes be clearer.
A query in FROM acts as a derived table in systems supporting the syntax.
The inner query calculates totals; the outer query filters them. Aliases for derived tables are required in many contexts and are good practice.
A JOIN combines related rows from tables. A subquery creates a result that another query can use. Either can sometimes express the same logic.
Use JOIN when columns from multiple tables are needed in the output or the relationship is central to the result.
Use EXISTS when the question is whether a related record exists and duplicate outer rows should not multiply because of one-to-many relationships.
Use a scalar subquery when one value, such as an average or maximum, is needed.
Do not assume subqueries are always slower than joins. Modern optimizers transform many equivalent expressions. Prioritize correctness and clarity, then measure performance on representative data.

sec.s: A view is a named query that can be queried like a table.

b.x: A view is a named query that can be queried like a table. A conventional view generally stores its definition rather than a separate copy of the query result. When queried, the database uses the view definition to produce results.

x: Simplification: complex joins and filters can be hidden behind a clear name.
Reuse: multiple queries can use the same definition.
Consistency: shared logic can reduce differences among applications.
Abstraction: users can work with a logical representation rather than every underlying table.
Restricted exposure: a view may expose selected columns or rows when permissions are configured appropriately.
Compatibility: a view can sometimes provide a stable interface as underlying tables evolve.

b.x: A view can help limit data exposure by presenting only approved fields. But creating a view alone does not guarantee security. Permissions must prevent users from bypassing the view and accessing underlying tables directly.
Some views are updatable, while others are not. Complex views containing joins, aggregates, grouping, DISTINCT, or computed expressions may have restrictions. Rules vary by DBMS.
A simple view based on one table may be updatable in many DBMS products:

Whether INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE through the view is allowed depends on the DBMS and view definition. Treat reporting views as read-only unless update behavior has been explicitly designed and tested.
This generally removes the view definition, not the underlying table data. IF EXISTS is supported by many systems, but verify the syntax for the chosen DBMS.
An ordinary view usually stores a query definition and calculates results when queried.

A materialized view stores the query result physically in systems that support it. It can speed up expensive reports but needs a refresh strategy to remain accurate. Support and syntax differ by DBMS; SQLite does not provide native materialized views in the same manner as some server databases.

sec.s: A stored procedure is a named routine stored in a database system that can perform one or more operations.

b.x: A stored procedure is a named routine stored in a database system that can perform one or more operations. Procedures may accept input parameters, return output values or result sets, perform validation, and coordinate database logic.

Stored procedures are supported by several database systems, but their syntax and capabilities differ. MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle provide stored-procedure features. PostgreSQL supports functions and procedures with its own language and rules. SQLite does not provide server-style stored procedures in the same way as those systems.

x: Reuse: common operations can be defined once.
Encapsulation: applications call a named operation instead of duplicating its internal steps.
Permission control: in supported configurations, users may execute a procedure without broad direct table permissions.
Consistency: shared business logic can reduce differences among applications.
Transaction handling: procedures can coordinate related operations where supported.
Reduced network round trips: several operations may be performed in one call.

b.x: Stored procedures are not automatically faster or safer in every situation. Poorly written procedures can still contain bugs, inefficient queries, or injection vulnerabilities.

x: Return a success or failure result.

b.x: Foreign keys and UNIQUE constraints should still be used where appropriate. Application rules and database constraints complement one another.
The exact syntax is DBMS-specific. This is a MySQL-style illustration, not portable SQL:
The input parameter is used as a value rather than concatenated into SQL text. Do not copy this syntax directly into SQLite or another DBMS without adapting it.

A procedure can be part of a least-privilege design. For example, an application account may be allowed to execute a specific procedure but not directly update every table. This depends on the DBMS's execution-permission model, ownership, security context, and configuration.

sec.s: A trigger is a database object that automatically executes a defined action when a specified event occurs.

b.x: A trigger is a database object that automatically executes a defined action when a specified event occurs. Common events include INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. Timing may be BEFORE, AFTER, or INSTEAD OF depending on the DBMS and trigger type.
Triggers can support auditing, maintain derived information, enforce certain business rules, or react to data changes. Their syntax and capabilities vary among products.

x: Record that a row was changed.
Prevent a change that violates a special rule.

b.x: Triggers should be used carefully. Hidden side effects can make applications harder to debug, and triggers may interact with other triggers or constraints.

x: AFTER UPDATE OF name ON Student

b.x: When the name of a Student row is updated, the trigger records the old and new names. In SQLite row-level triggers, OLD and NEW refer to row values before and after the operation as appropriate to the event.
The audit row should show the previous and new names, assuming the trigger and table were created successfully.

A BEFORE trigger runs before the triggering operation is completed according to the DBMS's semantics. An AFTER trigger runs after the operation. INSTEAD OF triggers can intercept operations on views in systems that support them.
Do not assume every DBMS allows the same actions inside every trigger type. Some products restrict modification of the row being changed in certain trigger types.
For row-level triggers, OLD commonly refers to previous row values and NEW to new values, but their availability depends on the event:

x: INSERT: NEW values exist; there is no previous row.
DELETE: OLD values exist; there is no new row.
UPDATE: OLD and NEW values are available in systems supporting this model.

b.x: Exact syntax and behavior differ across products.

x: Can support rules regardless of which application performs a write.
Side effects may be invisible to application developers.
Trigger chains can cause unexpected behavior.
Poorly written triggers can hurt performance.
Audit triggers may capture sensitive information and require protection.
Triggers do not replace proper constraints.

b.x: A stored procedure is a named routine called explicitly by an application, user, or another routine.
A trigger fires automatically in response to a configured database event.
A procedure is appropriate when an application requests a specific operation. A trigger is appropriate when an action should occur automatically whenever a particular event happens.

sec.s: SQL injection is a vulnerability in which untrusted input changes the structure or meaning of a SQL statement.

b.x: SQL injection is a vulnerability in which untrusted input changes the structure or meaning of a SQL statement. It often occurs when an application builds a query by concatenating user input directly into SQL text.

x: Reading data the user should not see.

b.x: Impact depends on the query, DBMS permissions, application architecture, and database account privileges.
Imagine a login form with username and password fields. Unsafe application code might construct a query by inserting supplied values directly into the SQL string.

x: query = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE username = '" + username + \

b.x: The input is treated as part of the SQL program itself. An attacker may supply characters that change the query's syntax or logic.
The core problem is mixing code and data without a reliable separation mechanism.
15.3 Why input filtering alone is insufficient
Removing quotation marks or blocking a few suspicious strings is fragile because:

x: SQL syntax differs across DBMS products.
Encoding and escaping rules can be complicated.
Attackers may find alternate input forms.
New query paths may bypass the filter.
Valid user input may be incorrectly rejected.
Security would depend on every code path applying identical filters correctly.

b.x: Input validation remains useful for checking business rules and expected formats, but it should not be the primary SQL injection defense.

sec.s: A parameterized query separates SQL statement structure from values supplied by the user.

b.x: A parameterized query separates SQL statement structure from values supplied by the user. The application provides SQL with placeholders and binds values through the database driver's parameter interface.
The driver or DBMS treats bound values as data, not SQL syntax. This prevents a value from changing the query structure in the way that direct string concatenation can.
Parameterized queries are the primary recommended defense for ordinary database access.

x: query = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE username = '" + username + "'"
    "SELECT user_id, username FROM Users WHERE username = ?",

b.x: The question mark is a placeholder used by Python's sqlite3 interface. The value is passed separately as a one-element tuple. The comma matters: (username,) is a tuple, while (username) is just the value in parentheses.
The SQL structure stays fixed. If the username contains quotation marks or SQL-looking text, the driver binds it as a value rather than interpreting it as SQL syntax.
Do not build this SQL by inserting values into the string using concatenation or formatting.
The first parameter supplies the new age; the second identifies the row.
This keeps the SQL structure separate from the identifier value.
Placeholder styles depend on the database driver

x: Some drivers use named placeholders such as :name.
Some drivers use %s as a placeholder token, but the driver binds the value; it is not ordinary Python string interpolation.

b.x: Follow the database driver's parameter style. Do not replace placeholders using string formatting.
16.7 Parameters represent values, not arbitrary SQL structure

A parameter normally cannot stand for a table name, column name, keyword, or sort direction. For example, SELECT * FROM ? does not usually work as intended. A placeholder is for a value, not a table identifier.
If the query must choose from several tables or sort columns, select the identifier from a strict allowlist controlled by the application. Never concatenate arbitrary user-supplied SQL identifiers.

x: query = f"SELECT student_id, name, age FROM Student ORDER BY {column}"

b.x: The inserted identifier comes from an allowlist, not arbitrary input. Values in filters should still be bound as parameters.

A parameterized query protects SQL structure from untrusted values, but it does not decide whether a user may access a particular record. A safely parameterized query could still expose another student's information if the application does not check authorization.

sec.t: Stored Procedures and SQL Injection Defense
sec.s: Stored procedures can help when they use parameters and keep query structure separate from input values.

b.x: 17.1 Can stored procedures prevent SQL injection?

Stored procedures can help when they use parameters and keep query structure separate from input values. However, a procedure is not automatically immune to injection. It can still be vulnerable if it builds dynamic SQL by concatenating untrusted input.
The important principle is safe query construction and parameter binding, not simply storing code inside the database.

x: Uses parameters in static SQL where possible.
Avoids building query strings from untrusted values.
Uses safe dynamic-SQL parameter binding when dynamic SQL is necessary.
Handles errors without exposing sensitive internal details.

b.x: Even if an injection vulnerability exists, impact can be reduced by limiting database permissions:

x: A reporting account should not be able to drop tables.
A read-only feature should not use an unrestricted write account.
An application should not connect as database administrator for ordinary requests.
Separate services can use separate accounts with narrowly scoped permissions.

b.x: Least privilege is defense in depth. It does not make unsafe query construction acceptable.

Detailed database errors can expose schema names, query fragments, table names, and implementation details. Log useful diagnostic information securely for developers while returning safe, appropriately generic messages to end users.
Do not suppress every error silently, because that can hide failed operations and integrity problems. Use secure logging and safe user-facing messages.

sec.s: Validation enforces business rules but does not replace parameterized queries.

x: IDs should have the expected format.
Numeric values should fall within reasonable ranges.
Status values should belong to approved options.
Text lengths should be limited appropriately.

b.x: Validation enforces business rules but does not replace parameterized queries.
Use PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, and NOT NULL where appropriate. These protect data integrity even when multiple application paths write to the database.

Give each database account only the permissions needed. Do not use an administrator account for ordinary web requests. Separate read-only reporting, application writes, migrations, and administrative tasks where appropriate.
Apply security updates to the DBMS, drivers, application framework, and operating system. Outdated components may contain known vulnerabilities.

Do not hard-code database passwords in publicly shared source code. Use protected configuration or a suitable secrets-management method. Restrict access to configuration and rotate credentials if exposure is suspected.

For remote database connections, use secure network configuration and encryption in transit where supported and required. Avoid exposing a database service directly to the public internet without a justified design and strong controls.

Retrieve only the columns and rows needed. Avoid SELECT * in sensitive application paths if it could expose additional fields as the schema changes. Do not return password hashes, internal tokens, or private data unnecessarily.

Passwords should not be stored as plaintext. Use a suitable password-hashing scheme designed for password storage, with appropriate parameters and salts, following current security guidance. Credential verification should follow a secure authentication design.

Monitor unusual database errors, unexpected access patterns, and suspicious activity. Logs should not unnecessarily contain passwords, session tokens, or sensitive personal information. Protect logs from unauthorized access and tampering.
Maintain secure backups and test restoration. Backups may contain all the sensitive data held in the main database, so protect them accordingly. Document and test recovery procedures.
Use transactions for operations that must succeed or fail together. Transactions help preserve consistency but do not replace authorization or safe query construction.

sec.s: Revision checklist

b.x: Relational algebra provides formal operations for manipulating relations. Selection, represented by σ, chooses rows that satisfy a condition. Projection, represented by π, chooses attributes or columns. Joins combine related rows from tables, allowing information to be retrieved across a relational schema. SQL implements these ideas through WHERE, SELECT, JOIN, and other query constructs, while adding practical features such as NULL, duplicate handling, and database-specific syntax.

SQL commands define structures and manipulate data. CREATE defines objects, ALTER changes structures, and DROP removes objects. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes existing rows, and DELETE removes rows. SELECT retrieves data. WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY controls result ordering, and GROUP BY supports aggregation.

Nested queries allow one query to use another query's result. IN tests membership in a set, EXISTS tests whether a matching row exists, and correlated subqueries refer to the outer query. Views package a query under a name and can simplify access to data. Stored procedures are explicitly invoked routines supported by many database systems. Triggers execute automatically when configured database events occur. Their exact syntax and capabilities depend on the DBMS; SQLite does not provide server-style stored procedures in the same way as many server databases.

SQL injection occurs when untrusted input changes the structure or meaning of a SQL statement. The primary defense for ordinary database queries is to use parameterized queries or prepared statements, binding values separately from SQL text. Input validation, database constraints, safe error handling, least privilege, secure credential management, updates, monitoring, and tested backups add further layers of protection.

The most important practical habit is to separate code from data. Do not build SQL by concatenating untrusted values. Use the parameter-binding interface provided by the database driver. When dynamic table or column names are required, select them from a strict allowlist. Stored procedures can support security when designed correctly, but they are not automatically safe. Query safety, data integrity, authentication, and authorization are distinct concerns; a dependable application needs all of them.
